source.passage: Microfinance was heralded as a tool for lifting the poor out of poverty by extending small business loans to those whom banks ignore. Rigorous evaluations have tempered that promise. Across randomized trials, access to microcredit rarely raised household income or consumption and seldom expanded businesses beyond subsistence scale. Yet the studies converge on a subtler benefit: borrowers gained flexibility in the timing of their spending, smoothing consumption across lean and flush periods and financing lumpy purchases they could not otherwise have afforded. The value of microcredit, the evidence suggests, lies not in generating new wealth but in rearranging the wealth households already have across time—a real service, though not the transformative engine of enterprise its champions once described.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the passage's characterization of microcredit's benefit?
choices: Households that received microloans started markedly more new businesses than otherwise similar households that received no loans.
Microloan borrowers reported greater trust in formal financial institutions after repayment, and were likelier than non-borrowers to open a savings account.
Regions served by many microfinance institutions had lower overall poverty rates a decade later than otherwise similar regions where such lenders stayed scarce.
Borrowers with microloans were no more likely than non-borrowers to raise their annual income but were better able to cover irregular, lumpy expenses.
source.key: Borrowers with microloans were no more likely than non-borrowers to raise their annual income but were better able to cover irregular, lumpy expenses.

adapted.passage: Microloans are small loans for people whom banks turn away. People once hoped these loans would lift families out of poverty by helping them start businesses. Careful studies have cooled that hope. Most borrowers did not earn more, and their businesses rarely grew past a very small size. But the studies agree on a quieter benefit. The loans helped families with the timing of their spending. Families could get through lean months and pay for big, one-time costs they could not have managed otherwise. Microloans, the evidence suggests, do not create new wealth. Instead, they help families spread the money they already have across time.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would best support the passage's idea of how microloans help?
choices: Families with microloans started far more new businesses than similar families without loans.
After repaying, borrowers trusted banks more and more often opened savings accounts.
Areas with many lenders had less poverty ten years later than areas with few.
Borrowers earned no more than others but could better pay big, one-time costs.
adapted.key: Borrowers earned no more than others but could better pay big, one-time costs.

source.passage: The transition to agriculture is routinely narrated as an obvious upgrade: farming produced more food, so foragers naturally adopted it. Skeletal evidence complicates the story. The bones of early farmers show, relative to the foragers who preceded them, shorter stature, more dental disease, and more markers of nutritional stress—hardly the profile of a population that had traded up. Agriculture did yield more calories per acre, but those calories came from a narrower range of starchy staples, purchased with longer labor and denser settlement that bred infection. Why, then, did anyone farm? The likeliest answer is not that farming was better but that, once populations had grown around it, returning to foraging could no longer feed them. Agriculture may have been less a prize that foragers seized than a trap that closed behind them—advantageous to the group's numbers even as it diminished the individual's health.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's characterization of the shift to agriculture?
choices: Some forager groups living beside farming villages declined to take up agriculture for many centuries.
The earliest farming settlements were far larger and more densely settled than the forager camps that preceded them on the same land.
Skeletons from the first farming communities show greater height and fewer stress markers than neighboring foragers'.
Early crops delivered several times more calories per acre than the wild foods gathered from the same land.
source.key: Skeletons from the first farming communities show greater height and fewer stress markers than neighboring foragers'.

adapted.passage: Many people see farming as an obvious upgrade. Farming made more food, so foragers gladly took it up. Ancient bones tell a different story. But those calories came from a few starchy crops, and they cost longer hours of work. Crowded villages also spread disease. So why farm at all? Perhaps once populations had grown, foraging could no longer feed everyone. Farming may have been less a prize than a trap: good for the group's numbers, but bad for each person's health.

choices: Some forager groups next to farming villages refused to farm for many centuries.

source.passage: Bilingual children are frequently said to enjoy a general "executive-function advantage"—better attention control and task-switching—attributed to the constant effort of managing two languages. Early studies reported such advantages, but a skeptic notes that these findings came disproportionately from small samples and were more likely to be published when the effect was positive. She hypothesizes that the reported advantage is inflated by this publication filter rather than reflecting a robust cognitive difference, and predicts a specific signature in the literature if she is right.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the skeptic's hypothesis?
choices: Large, pre-registered studies find little or no bilingual advantage, while the positive results cluster among smaller studies.
Bilingual adults outperform monolingual adults on some attention tasks but not on others, with the gap appearing mainly on tasks that demand rapid switching.
Children who begin a second language earlier show larger executive-function advantages than those who begin later, a dose-response pattern across ages.
Monolingual children can improve their executive function through several weeks of targeted attention training.
source.key: Large, pre-registered studies find little or no bilingual advantage, while the positive results cluster among smaller studies.

adapted.passage: Many people say that children who speak two languages are better at focusing. They are also said to switch between tasks more easily. The idea is that juggling two languages trains the brain. Early studies seemed to agree. But one scientist doubts it. She points out that many of those studies were small. She also notes that a study was more likely to be published when it found an advantage. She thinks this publishing pattern made the advantage look bigger than it really is. If she is right, she says, the research should show a telltale pattern.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the scientist's idea?
choices: Large, planned studies find little advantage; most positive results come from small studies.
Bilingual adults do better on some focus tasks but not others, mostly ones that need fast switching.
Children who start a second language earlier show bigger advantages than later starters.
Children who speak one language can improve their focus with weeks of special training.
adapted.key: Large, planned studies find little advantage; most positive results come from small studies.

source.passage: The reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone has become the textbook illustration of a trophic cascade: with wolves back, elk abandon the exposed streamside groves where they are easily ambushed, browsing pressure eases, and willows and aspen surge back along the banks. Recent fieldwork, however, has questioned how clean the story really is. Willow recovery across the park has proved distinctly patchy. It has been vigorous where beaver dams raise the water table and keep the banks wet, and feeble or absent where those conditions are lacking—even in places where wolves are plainly present and elk are plainly wary. The predators' return, this work suggests, may well be a necessary ingredient of the recovery credited to it, but it is just as plainly not a sufficient one.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the revisionist claim that the return of the wolves was not sufficient to produce the vegetation recovery?
choices: Elk populations fell sharply in the years immediately after wolves were reintroduced.
Beaver colonies increased across much of the park following the reintroduction of wolves.
Wolves hunted elk most successfully in the open bottoms of river valleys, where the browsing herds had few routes of escape.
Willow stands failed to recover where water tables were low, despite a heavy and sustained wolf presence.
source.key: Willow stands failed to recover where water tables were low, despite a heavy and sustained wolf presence.

adapted.passage: Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park. The park then became a famous example of a chain reaction in nature. With wolves back, elk stayed away from open stream banks where they could be ambushed. With less elk grazing, willow and aspen trees grew back along the streams. Newer fieldwork suggests the story is not so simple. Willows have recovered unevenly. They came back strongly where beaver dams raise the water and keep the banks wet. They did poorly where the banks stayed dry, even where wolves were clearly present and elk were clearly cautious. Wolves may be needed for the recovery, but they are not enough on their own.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most support the newer claim that the wolves' return was not enough by itself to bring the trees back?
choices: Elk numbers dropped sharply in the years right after wolves were brought back.
Beaver colonies grew across much of the park after wolves were brought back.
Wolves caught elk most often in open valleys, where herds had few escape routes.
Willows failed where water was low, despite many wolves living there for years.
adapted.key: Willows failed where water was low, despite many wolves living there for years.

source.passage: The idea that bringing hostile groups into contact will erode their prejudices has an appealing simplicity, and decades of studies confirm that contact often does reduce bias. The finding is real; the simplicity is deceptive. Early researchers were explicit that contact helps only when certain conditions hold—when the groups meet as equals, pursue shared goals, and act with institutional support. Absent these, contact can as easily entrench hostility as dissolve it, as anyone who has watched rival factions share cramped quarters can attest. Later analyses complicate the picture further: some of the prejudice-reducing effect appears to spread to group members never actually encountered, while some evaporates once the structured setting is left behind. The evidence thus supports a claim narrower than the slogan—that contact of a particular, engineered kind reliably reduces prejudice—and warns against the broader inference that mere exposure will do the work on its own.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the passage's central claim?
choices: Evidence that a program meeting the classic conditions—equal status, shared goals, institutional support—sharply reduced participants' bias
A finding that reductions in prejudice from contact tend to fade once participants leave the structured setting
A large study showing that people who merely lived alongside an out-group, with no shared goals or institutional support, developed durably lower prejudice
A study showing that contact under unequal, competitive conditions increased hostility between groups
source.key: A large study showing that people who merely lived alongside an out-group, with no shared goals or institutional support, developed durably lower prejudice

adapted.passage: Many people believe that time together makes rival groups less prejudiced. Decades of studies show that contact often does reduce bias. But the idea is not that simple. Without these, contact can make hostility worse. Later studies also found that some of the benefit fades once people leave the planned setting. So the evidence supports a narrower claim. Carefully planned contact reduces prejudice. Simply being around another group will not do the job by itself.

choices: Groups meeting as equals, with shared goals and their leaders' support, became far less biased.
Drops in prejudice from contact faded soon after people left the planned setting.

Contact between unequal, competing groups made the two groups more hostile to each other.
adapted.key: People who just lived near another group, with no goals or support, grew lastingly less biased.

source.passage: The famous 'marshmallow test'—in which young children who resisted an immediate treat for a larger delayed one later showed better life outcomes—is widely read as evidence that self-control is a stable trait that shapes a child's future. A reconsideration questions the direction of the lesson. Waiting, researchers point out, is only rational when the promise of a reward is credible; a child who has learned that adults' assurances often go unmet acts sensibly by taking the sure thing now. When experimenters first demonstrated that they were reliable, children waited far longer, and when they proved unreliable, previously 'patient' children grabbed the treat at once. On this reading, the test may measure not willpower but a child's evidence-based expectation about whether the world keeps its promises—an expectation that tracks the stability of the environment the child comes from.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the reconsideration described in the text?
choices: Children who waited longer for the treat scored higher on personality measures of conscientiousness years later, and the association held even after researchers adjusted for how stable the child's household had been.
Older children, on average, waited longer for the delayed reward than younger children did, and the difference widened with each additional year of age.
Children raised in households with unpredictable access to food waited less than peers from stable households, even when the two groups scored equally on independent tests of self-control.
Children who had just watched the experimenter break a promise waited as long for the second treat as children who had watched her keep one, whatever the stability of the household they came from.
source.key: Children raised in households with unpredictable access to food waited less than peers from stable households, even when the two groups scored equally on independent tests of self-control.

adapted.passage: In the famous "marshmallow test," young children could eat one treat now or wait for two treats later. Those who waited did better later in life. A child who has learned that adults often break promises is being sensible by taking the sure treat. When experimenters first showed they were reliable, children waited much longer. When they proved unreliable, even "patient" children grabbed the treat at once. The test may measure not willpower but whether a child expects promises to be kept. That depends on how stable the child's home has been.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most support the researchers' new view of the test?
choices: Longer waiters were more responsible years later, even counting how stable their homes were.
Older children waited longer than younger ones, and the gap grew with each year.

adapted.key: Children from homes often short on food waited less, despite equal self-control test scores.

source.passage: When a cleaner wrasse, marked with a colored spot, scraped its body against surfaces after seeing itself in a mirror, some researchers hailed the fish as self-aware, extending to it a capacity long reserved for apes and dolphins. Caution is warranted. Passing the mark test may show only that an animal can associate a mirror reflection with its own body, a sensorimotor achievement that need not involve any concept of a self. The wrasse's ecology supplies a simpler reading: a fish whose living depends on detecting blemishes on other bodies might be primed to respond to a blemish wherever a reflection places it, with no inner spectator required. To infer rich self-awareness from the behavior is to assume that one impressive performance can be produced only by the most demanding mechanism—when a leaner one, well suited to the animal's way of life, will do.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's alternative explanation of the wrasse's behavior?
choices: Wrasses try to remove marks placed on their own bodies even when the marks resemble nothing they encounter while cleaning other fish.
Cleaner wrasses are unusually quick to notice the small blemishes on the bodies of the fish they clean.
Cleaner wrasses spend more time in front of a mirror than other reef fish placed in the same tank do.
Apes and dolphins scrape at a marked spot far more consistently than cleaner wrasses do when the same mark test is administered to both.
source.key: Wrasses try to remove marks placed on their own bodies even when the marks resemble nothing they encounter while cleaning other fish.

This fish gets its food by finding spots on other fish and picking them off. So it may be ready to react to a spot wherever it sees one, even in a mirror.

source.passage: The printing press is celebrated as the engine of mass literacy, as though cheaper books had straightforwardly taught Europe to read. The chronology resists the compliment. For its first century and more, print largely served readers who already existed—clergy, jurists, merchants—and the commonest products of the early presses were not primers but liturgical works and learned tomes in Latin, a language most Europeans could not read at all. Literacy rates in many regions barely moved until the confessional campaigns and schooling drives of later centuries gave ordinary people both a reason to read and the instruction to do so. Print made those later expansions cheaper to sustain, but it did not by itself supply the motive or the teaching that literacy requires. The press was a necessary instrument of the reading public that eventually formed; it was not, on its own, the cause of that public's formation.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument?
choices: Across Europe the total number of books in circulation multiplied many times over within a few decades of the first printed editions.
In regions that adopted printing early, literacy rose sharply only generations later, once church-led schooling campaigns began.
Early printers competed fiercely for the trade in Latin editions of the classical authors.
Literacy rose fastest in the first decades after the press appeared, well before any schooling campaigns began.
source.key: In regions that adopted printing early, literacy rose sharply only generations later, once church-led schooling campaigns began.

adapted.passage: The printing press is often praised for teaching Europe to read, as if cheaper books alone made people readers. The timeline does not support that story. In many regions, reading rates barely changed until much later, when church campaigns and school programs gave ordinary people a reason to read and lessons in how to do it. Printing made those later efforts cheaper. On its own, though, it supplied neither the reason nor the teaching.

source.passage: When narrow gullies were photographed on Martian crater walls, they were quickly read as the fingerprints of flowing water, and thus of a planet perhaps hospitable to life. The channels do resemble those water carves on Earth. But resemblance is not mechanism. Many of the gullies lie in places too cold for liquid water to persist, and their activity peaks not in the Martian summer but in the depths of winter, when carbon-dioxide frost accumulates and then sublimates. A growing number of planetary scientists therefore suspect the sculptor is not water at all but blocks of dry ice, lubricated by the gas they release as they slide. If so, the gullies say little about Mars's habitability.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the carbon-dioxide hypothesis over the water hypothesis?
choices: The Martian gullies closely resemble the channels that seasonal runoff cuts in desert slopes on Earth.
Clay minerals that form only after prolonged exposure to liquid water have been identified in ancient terrain far from the gullies.
Time-lapse imaging shows gully material moving during the coldest months, when CO2 frost is present but liquid water cannot exist.
The gullies sit on slopes steep enough for loose debris to slide under gravity alone, without any lubricant.
source.key: Time-lapse imaging shows gully material moving during the coldest months, when CO2 frost is present but liquid water cannot exist.

adapted.passage: When photos showed narrow gullies on the walls of craters on Mars, many people thought flowing water had carved them. If so, Mars might once have been friendly to life. The gullies do look like channels that water cuts on Earth. But looking alike does not prove the same cause. Many of the gullies sit in places too cold for liquid water to last. They are also most active in the middle of winter, not in summer. That is when frozen carbon dioxide, called dry ice, builds up and then turns straight into gas. So many scientists now think the gullies were carved by blocks of dry ice sliding on the gas they give off.

adapted.key: Photos show gully rock moving in the coldest months, when dry ice forms and any water would be frozen solid.

source.passage: That a warming planet might make part of Europe colder sounds contradictory, yet it follows from the physics of ocean circulation. The Atlantic conveyor that carries tropical heat northward is driven partly by the sinking of cold, salty water in the far North Atlantic. As Greenland's ice melts, it floods that region with fresh water, which is less dense and sinks less readily; the circulation slows, and less tropical heat reaches northwestern Europe. The claim is carefully hedged. Researchers do not predict a new ice age, nor that regional cooling would offset global warming overall—the planet keeps warming. They argue only that a global mean temperature can conceal opposing regional trends, and that a warming world is compatible with, and could even produce, a cooler northwestern Europe.
source.prompt: Which observation would most support the mechanism described in the text?
choices: Average temperatures across Europe fell even as global average temperatures rose.
As freshwater flowing into the North Atlantic increased, the sinking of deep water slowed and the northward transport of heat weakened.
Greenland's ice sheet lost mass more rapidly during warmer years, shedding meltwater from its margins at rates that tracked each summer's temperatures.
Tropical ocean temperatures rose in step with the global average temperature.
source.key: As freshwater flowing into the North Atlantic increased, the sinking of deep water slowed and the northward transport of heat weakened.

adapted.passage: It sounds strange that a warming planet could make part of Europe colder, but the ocean explains how. A huge Atlantic current carries warm water from the tropics north toward Europe. The current is driven partly by cold, salty water sinking in the far North Atlantic. As Greenland's ice melts, it pours fresh water into that area. Fresh water is lighter, so it does not sink as easily. The current then slows, and less tropical heat reaches northwestern Europe. Scientists are careful about this claim. They do not predict a new ice age, and they agree that the planet as a whole keeps warming. They say only that a warmer world could still produce a cooler northwestern Europe.

Ocean water in the tropics warmed at the same pace as the world as a whole did.
adapted.key: As more fresh water flowed into the North Atlantic, deep water sank more slowly and less heat moved north.

source.passage: Standard narratives attribute Japan's swift industrialization after 1868 to the Meiji government's importation of Western machinery and foreign advisers. The hardware mattered, but it does not explain why Japan absorbed what other nineteenth-century states could not. Long before Commodore Perry, Tokugawa Japan possessed high literacy, a dense commercial network, sophisticated rural proto-industry, and merchant houses skilled in double-entry accounting and futures trading. These endowments meant that imported technology met a workforce and a managerial class already primed to deploy it. Foreign experts were, tellingly, dismissed as soon as Japanese personnel could replace them—often within a decade. The Meiji reformers' genuine innovation lay less in acquiring foreign techniques than in redirecting indigenous capacities toward national ends. Where historians once read the period as a story of borrowing, the more defensible reading treats borrowing as the visible surface of a deeper continuity, one that the drama of Westernization has tended to obscure.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's central claim?
choices: A neighboring state that imported identical Western machinery but lacked comparable commercial institutions failed to industrialize at a similar pace.
The Meiji government spent more on foreign machinery than any other contemporaneous Asian state.
Foreign advisers in Japan were paid substantially higher salaries than they had earned at home, a premium that drew engineers and accountants to Meiji ministries.
Tokugawa-era literacy rates were significantly lower in rural regions than in major cities.
source.key: A neighboring state that imported identical Western machinery but lacked comparable commercial institutions failed to industrialize at a similar pace.

adapted.passage: Most histories say Japan built factories quickly after 1868 for one reason. Its new Meiji government brought in Western machines and foreign advisers. The machines mattered, but they do not explain why Japan could put them to use when many other countries could not. Long before 1868, Japan already had high literacy, busy trade networks, and skilled village workshops. Its merchant houses kept careful account books. So the new machines met workers and managers who were ready to run them. Foreign experts were sent home as soon as Japanese workers could replace them, often within ten years. Japan's success came less from borrowing than from business skills it already had.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's main claim?
choices: A nearby country that bought the same machines but lacked those business skills built factories more slowly.
The Meiji government spent more on foreign machines than any other country in Asia did then.

adapted.key: A nearby country that bought the same machines but lacked those business skills built factories more slowly.

source.passage: The 'hygiene hypothesis' is popularly summarized as a simple warning: modern cleanliness, by depriving children of germs, leaves their immune systems untrained and prone to allergy. Immunologists have largely abandoned that formulation. The rise in allergic disease does not correlate well with reduced exposure to the common infectious agents of childhood—colds, flus, and the like—which the crude version implicates. It correlates instead with diminished contact with a particular set of ancient, largely harmless microorganisms, the so-called 'old friends' that co-evolved with humans and help calibrate immune regulation. On this refined account, the problem is not insufficient infection but the loss of specific symbiotic exposures; a childhood full of ordinary colds confers little protection, while contact with the right environmental microbes does. Cleanliness is not quite the villain the slogan suggests.
source.prompt: Which finding would most directly support the refined account over the popular version of the hygiene hypothesis?
choices: Children raised in unusually clean, nearly germ-free households had markedly higher rates of allergic disease than did children who grew up in ordinary, less sanitized homes.
Adults who contract frequent respiratory infections tend to have weaker immune systems overall than adults who rarely fall ill.
Children who suffered many ordinary childhood infections were no less allergic than those who suffered few, whereas children exposed to diverse environmental microbes were.
The 'old friend' microorganisms were far more common in the human environments of thousands of years ago than they are in the households of modern industrialized countries today.
source.key: Children who suffered many ordinary childhood infections were no less allergic than those who suffered few, whereas children exposed to diverse environmental microbes were.

adapted.passage: The "hygiene hypothesis" is often told as a simple warning. Modern homes are so clean that children meet few germs. As a result, their immune systems never learn properly, and allergies follow. Most immune scientists no longer accept that version. The rise in allergies does not match up well with fewer common childhood illnesses, such as colds and flu. Instead, it matches up with less contact with certain ancient, mostly harmless microbes. These "old friends" evolved alongside humans and help tune the immune system. In this newer view, a childhood full of colds gives little protection, while contact with the right microbes from the environment does.
adapted.prompt: Which finding would best support the newer view rather than the popular version?
choices: Children with many colds were no less allergic than those with few, but children living near varied microbes were.

adapted.key: Children with many colds were no less allergic than those with few, but children living near varied microbes were.
